5.2.name: 5.02.md
5.2.text: A block is a compound statement. That is, "a sequence of statements and declarations surrounded by a pair of curly braces." (p. 173) Moreover, a block is a scope. We can use it when our logic requires more than a single statement. Thus it allows us to group together a set of statements for sequential executions to achieve a logical task. A block can be used to define loops, if statements, functions, etc.

5.4.name: 5.04.md
5.4.text:
```cpp
(a) while (string::iterator iter != s.end()) { /* . . . */ }
(b) while (bool status = find(word)) { /* . . . */ }
```

(a) iter is declared in the scope of the while statement at every iteration of

the loop. Moreover, it used in loop's condition uninitialized. This an error. Also, a potential problem, is that the statement will loop forever, unless iter is changed within the body of the loop. Correction:

```cpp
string:iterator iter = s.begin();
while (iter != s.ed() { /* . . . */}
```

(b) the while loops as long as the result of the assignment returns true, which

```text
depends on the returned value of find() function.
```

5.8.name: 5.08.md
5.8.text: A dangling else occurs when there are more if clauses than else clauses in a nested if-else statement. The matching of the remaining else, i.e. dangling, with an if statement is ambiguous. C++ resolves this by matching each else clause with the closest preceding unmatched if clause. The use of explicit curly braces to delimits the scopes of the inner and outer if-else statements removes this ambiguity.

5.15.name: 5.15.md
5.15.text:
```cpp
(a) for (int ix = 0; ix != sz; ++ix) { /* . . . */ }
	if (ix != sz)
			// . . .
(b) int ix;
	for (ix != sz; ++ix) { /* . . . */ }
(c) for (int ix = 0; ix != sz; ++ix, ++ sz) { /* . . . */ }
```

(a) The loop presumably iterates through elements of a string, a vector or an

```cpp
array. It stops when the last element is reached. The if statements after the
loop checks if the container object has been read completely.
Issues: sz is uninitialized.
Correction:
	for (decltype(v.size()) ix = 0, sz = v.end(); ix != sz; ++ix) { /* ... */ }
```

(b) Does the same thing as a.

```cpp
Issues: missing initializing statement and both ix and sz
uninitialized.
Correction:
	for (decltype(v.size()) ix = 0, sz = v.end(); ix != sz; ++ix) { /* ... */ }
```

(c) Does the same thing as a.

```cpp
Issues: The condition will always be false; therefore, if
started, the loop will never terminate. This is so because sz is incremented at
the same rate as ix.  Again, sz is uninitialized.
Correction:
	for (decltype(v.size()) ix = 0, sz = v.end(); ix != sz; ++ix) { /* ... */ }
```
